messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his shoulders drawn inward, a posture that has become habitual over the past two years. At sixty-eight, he carries himself with the careful deliberation of someone who has learned not to trust his own body. His work as the director of a community health nonprofit has defined much of his adult life—decades spent building programs for vulnerable populations, advocating for those without voices. Now, ironically, he finds himself unable to speak about what happened to him.

The assault occurred during a solo camping trip in the mountains, something Marcus had done annually for thirty years. He had gone to clear his head after a difficult board meeting. A man approached him at dusk near the trail, asking for directions. Marcus, always helpful, always attuned to others' needs, stopped to assist. What followed was a violent attack that left him physically injured and psychologically shattered. He was found by another hiker the next morning.

In the weeks immediately following, Marcus did what he had always done—he functioned. He went to the hospital, gave a police statement, returned to work. His ex-wife, whom he remained cordial with, offered support that he politely declined. His adult children knew only the bare facts: their father had been assaulted during a camping trip. He didn't want to burden them with details. This compartmentalization worked for a while. Then, around month four, everything fractured.

Now, two years later, Marcus describes feeling like he exists behind glass. He goes through his workdays mechanically, attending meetings and reviewing grant proposals, but finds himself unable to engage with the human connection that once fueled his passion for the work. During staff meetings, he sometimes dissociates entirely, coming to awareness mid-sentence without knowing what he's been saying. His colleagues have noticed his withdrawal, though they attribute it to aging or burnout.

Sleep has become a battlefield. Most nights, Marcus lies awake until three or four in the morning, his mind cycling through intrusive images of that evening. When he does sleep, he wakes gasping, his sheets soaked with sweat. He's taken to sleeping in his living room chair rather than his bed, a change he doesn't fully understand but feels necessary. The darkness of his bedroom has become unbearable.

His body has become a stranger to him. Certain physical sensations—the feel of fabric against his skin, unexpected touch, even the pressure of his own hands—trigger waves of panic. He's lost fifteen pounds without trying, having difficulty with appetite and finding eating itself an act requiring conscious effort. He avoids the gym where he once exercised regularly, unable to tolerate the vulnerability of changing clothes or showering in public spaces.

What troubles Marcus most is the shame, a corrosive feeling that contradicts everything he intellectually understands about trauma. He works with trauma survivors; he knows the statistics, the neurobiology, the fact that assault is never the victim's fault. Yet he carries a deep, wordless conviction that somehow he should have known better, should have been more careful, should have been stronger. He finds himself hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him—scanning crowds, noting exits, feeling his heart race at unexpected sounds.

Marcus continues to show up to work, to answer emails, to maintain the facade of functionality. But underneath, he feels himself fragmenting, caught between the man he was and someone he no longer recognizes. He has finally, reluctantly, come to therapy, though he struggles to articulate why he's here or what he hopes might change.
